For 10 points, identify this ethnic group that frequently clashed with the Byzantine Empire over control of the Balkans, who Basil II is known for slaying.

John II of Brabant was besieged in Genappe castle for sheltering Jews by an army of the poor on their way to this city. A different city was depicted in a medieval map as a widow in black when Raymond Bertrand de Got moved from it to this city. Geoffrey Boucicaut ("boo-see-COE") besieged a building in this city for five years before Pedro Martinez de Luna escaped. An ecumenical council in this city excommunicated Raymond VI of Toulouse. (*) Laura de Noves, believed to be the "Laura" of Petrarch's works, was a native of this city. The potential loss of power that the War of the Eight Saints could have created for this city led to the accession of Robert of Geneva as Clement VII, whom many countries recognized over Gregory XI in Rome. For 10 points, name this southern French city home to the Papacy from 1309-1376.

After this event, the Hungarian-born Carlos Mardel argued against a "no change" option in favor of a "clean slate" option. A 60-question survey inquiring about local landforms and rivers formed the "Parochial Memories" distributed after this event. After this event, wooden cages inside buildings became common in a downtown area designed by Eugenio dos Santos. This event was called an act of divine providence against his country's sinful government by (*) Gabriel Malagrida. This event forced a ruler to move to a tent complex in Ajuda, where he was attacked in the Tavora affair three years later. After this event, the command to "bury the dead and heal the living" was proclaimed by the Marquis of Pombal, who served as Joseph I's chief minister. For 10 points, name this 1755 natural disaster that destroyed much of the capital of Portugal.
3.r: 1755 Lisbon earthquake [or the Great Lisbon earthquake; prompt on earthquake]

3.q: A holder of this position, who converted to Christianity after meeting a seer on the Isles of Scilly, legendarily slapped a queen known as "the Haughty" with his glove for refusing to convert. A holder of this position died after being wounded three times while fighting a peasant army at the Battle of Stiklestad. That holder of this position, from the Fairhair dynasty, established his country's national church with Bishop Grimkell and was (*) canonized after death. A holder of this position was killed while fighting against Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Stamford Bridge. Olaf Tryggvason and St. Olaf encouraged the Christianization of their country while holding this position. For 10 points, Harald Hardrada held what title as the ruler of a Scandinavian kingdom?
3.r: kings of Norway [or Norges Konge; prompt on ruler of Norway or similar] (The first line refers to Olaf Tryggvason and the second to St. Olaf.)

3.q: This region's native people worshipped at altars called irminsuls, and its territory was split into Ernestine and Albertine branches. This region was one of the (*) four secular electorates of the Holy Roman Empire, and it was ruled for most of its history by the House of Wettin. The Seven Years' War originated when Frederick the Great invaded this region, and this region led the neighboring state of Anhalt in a personal union. For ten points, name this German state with capital Dresden, whose namesake people underwent a migration with the Angles.

Description acceptable. A speech given at this event notes how a pirate called Alexander the Great a "Great Robber" in order to illustrate the unjustness of its perpetrators. The giver of that speech called up Dr. Juxon afterwards to show his Christianity. An apologetic memoir about this event's central victim, the Eikon Basilike, was so popular that John Milton was commissioned to write a response to it, Eikonoklastes. Henry (*) Ireton's Army Remonstrance called for this action to take place. This event took place at a makeshift scaffold in front of the Banqueting House. At this event, spectators could pay to dip their handkerchiefs in blood, and it occurred following its central figure's trial at by Solicitor General John Cook and other roundheads. For 10 points, name this event which saw a Stuart king executed by Oliver Cromwell after he lost the English Civil War.
3.r: Execution of Charles I [accept any answers involving the death of Charles I; prompt on Charles I or Charles]

3.q: Offenders had their hands chopped off for smuggling this good out of England in a practice known as "owling." The Hull merchant William de la Pole financed Edward II's wars in France with proceeds from this commodity, which was the subject of an export tax labeled the "Great Custom." Successful merchants financed a class of churches named for this commodity throughout the Cotswolds. King Edward III decreed that to be reminded of this inedible good's importance, the Lord Chancellor must sit on a (*) "sack" of this material while presiding over the House of Lords. The enclosure movement consolidated English farmland for the production of this commodity, whose industry declined in England with the rise of the Merino breed in Spain. For 10 points, name this fiber obtained from sheep.

This event was masterminded by two cabals of businessmen, Hugh MacRae's "Secret Nine" and Walker Taylor's "Group Six." A contributing factor was probably women's rights activist Rebecca Felton's endorsement of violence and a controversial editorial responding to it by Alex Manly of the Daily Record newspaper that openly discussed miscegenation. Future Navy Secretary Josephus Daniels has been called the "precipitator" of it for openly calling for an end to "Negro Domination." This incident occurred two days after the election of a Fusionist (*) mayor opposed by the Democratic Party. During this event, Colonel Alfred Waddell threatened to "choke the Cape Fear" with black "carcasses" as he led 2,000 citizens to turn out the mayor and biracial city council. For 10 points, name this only coup d'etat in United States history, an 1898 incident in which white supremacists seized a North Carolina port.
3.r: the Wilmington coup [or the Wilmington massacre; if you are a Southern apologist, accept Wilmington riot]

3.q: One saint from this country is credited with creating the Fifteen O's prayer and founded a namesake monastic order which was open to men and women. Laurentius Andreae played a key role in translating the Bible into the language of this country, and the Reformation was promoted here by the Petri brothers. One ruler of this country founded the Academy of Arcadia after converting to Catholicism and moving to Rome. It's not Ireland, but St. Bridget, one of the patron saints of Europe, hailed from this country. One leader of this country was advised by (*) Axel Oxenstierna and died at the Battle of Lutzen while intervening in the Thirty Year's War; that man was known as the Lion of the North. The Vasa dynasty once ruled, for 10 points, what Lutheran Scandinavian country whose most famous ruler was Gustavus Adolphus?
3.c: 2014 SUBMIT Pkt 11. Washington, Dartmouth B, GW A Q4

3.q: A popular song accused the losing commander at this battle of fleeing "like a frightened bird, chased from its nest in the morning." Due to differing speeds of advance, the battle line of one army had formed a V-shape at the beginning of this battle. The winning army at this battle began marching around the flank of their enemies at 4 AM; two hours later, the British pickets were surprised by a dawn assault from the east. Reinforcements that had been dispatched to aid the loser of this battle got lost shortly after leaving (*) Edinburgh Castle. The Hanoverian commander at this battle, John Cope, was later accused of cowardice, but cleared by a court-martial. For 10 points, name this first major battle of the Forty-Five, a victory for the Jacobites under Bonnie Prince Charlie.
3.c: 2015 Chicago Open History Pkt 09 Ebner Q4

3.q: The leader of this region expanded its territory through the Stairs Expedition. It was divided into two economic zones: the Free Trade Zone and Private Domain and its armed forces were referred to as the Public Force. Two men who played a major role in the downfall of this polity were Emile Vandervelde and E.D. Morel, who published several articles about this polity in the magazine Speaker. A diplomat, who would eventually be executed because of his role in the (*) Easter Uprising, prepared a document detailing the horrific conditions in this polity, which is referred to as the Casement Report. Its leader's establishment of The International African Association catalyzed the creation of this state, which came to fruition in the Berlin Conference. Serving as the inspiration for Conrad's Heart of Darkness, for 10 points, name this polity, which existed from 1885 - 1908, that was ruled by Leopold II.

Women among this group could benefit from "prefection," in which the king legally designated them as a son so they could inherit property. A member of this group, Amadeus Aba, led a breakaway state after most of its members failed to recognize the legitimacy of king Charles Robert. Before the Counter-Reformation, members of this group converted en masse to Lutheranism and Calvinism at the encouragement of Gabriel Bethlen. This group was granted the right of resistance by the Golden Bull of 1222 issued by king (*) Andrew II. In an early implementation of "salami tactics," the privileges of this group were abolished in 1947 by a Communist government. This group was swelled with ranks of immigrant Frankish and German knights called advena during the reign of the Arpad dynasty. For 10 points, identify this unusually numerous elite class of people in a Central European kingdom governed from Budapest.
3.r: Hungarian nobility [or Magyar nobility; accept Hungarian knights or Magyar knights; accept equivalents for “nobility” such as nobles; accept Hungarian barons or főnemesség; accept Transylvanian for “Hungarian”; prompt on Hungarians or Magyars; prompt on nobility or nobles or barons]

3.q: One group that was formed in response to this event eventually splintered off into another group called HZDS and later changed its name to the Civic Democratic Union. That group was the Public Against Violence, which was analogous to another country's Civic Forum and this event would be immortalized on 2-Euro coin by a set of jingling keys. The actions of an undercover StB agent during this event may have helped to gain steam by falsifying the death of Martin Smid. The event began on International (*) Students Day and marked the 50th anniversary of the death of a student at the hands of the Nazis. Much of this event was fomented by actors in theaters and it received support from the likes of Cardinal Frantisek Tomasek and members of Charter 77 including Vaclav Havel. Occurring a week after the fall of the Berlin Wall, for 10 points, name this 1989 bloodless revolution that led to democratic elections in Czechoslovakia.

The first version of these annals was published by Abraham Wheloc at Cambridge in 1644, and was expanded upon by Edmund Gibson's edition 49 years later. A single leaf preserving part of these annals is known as the Cottonian Fragment. The youngest of the nine surviving manuscript copies of these annals is named for Peterborough Abbey, and covers the events of the Anarchy and the reign of King Stephen. These annals were compiled beginning during the reign of (*) Alfred the Great, and draw on Bede and other sources to describe British history. For 10 points, name this historical chronicle which is named for two Germanic peoples who settled Britain.
3.c: 2019 Guerrilla History Pkt 3 -- Alston + Christensen + Myers Q13

3.q: Immense Nazi demands of wine from this region led to one of its major producers walling up reserves of its 1928 vintage, a well-known favorite of Winston Churchill. Frustrated with the onset of the Phylloxera epidemic and the importation of grapes from other regions, wine producers in this region rioted in 1911, burning much of the town of Ay (ah-EE). The founder of a famous wine producer in this region served as mayor of Paris when it was liberated from Nazi rule. Breaking from the trend in the 19th century for wines from this region to be sweet, producer (*) Perrier-Jouet produced a dry wine that critics called brut ("brute") for its perceived severity. Though he strove to remove the best-known quality of wines from this region, they grew in quality as innovations in pruning, harvesting, and pressing were pioneered by Dom Perignon. For 10 points, name this French region that has become synonymous with sparkling wine.

A holder of this position fathered the only Hungarian king named Peter. A particularly unpleasant person in this position attempted to secure power by marrying a slaveholding Lombard noblewoman named Waldrada and was burned to death by his subjects. A long-time holder of this position was exiled along with his son by the Council of Ten. The silver (*) grosso coin was introduced by a holder of this position to pay for a campaign that sacked Zadar and Zara. The official vehicle for many holders of this position, the Bucentaur, was a barge from which they threw a ring into the ocean to symbolically marry the sea. A blind holder of it diverted the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople. For 10 points, name this position of leadership by which Enrico Dandolo ruled Venice.

Description acceptable. One radio station during this period issued broadcasts bookended with coded information as part of its "personal messages." In the aftermath of this period, thousands were tried for "national unworthiness" as part of the "legal purge" and the "savage purge." A woman punished for engaging in "horizontal collaboration" during this period was the subject of a photograph by Robert Capa. The (*) Vel D'Hiv ("vell-deev") Roundup was carried out during this period by a government opposed by guerilla groups known as the maquis. At the start of this period, one leader issued the Appeal of 18 June to galvanize resistance cells later organized under Jean Moulin. For 10 points, name this period during which the Vichy government was established in one country following its fall to the Nazis in 1940.
3.r: German occupation of France [accept word forms indicating France under the rule of Nazi Germany; accept the Military Administration in France; accept Vichy France or the Vichy period before read; prompt on World War II or the Second World War or the 1940s]

3.q: In Emesa, this group stripped a lead and copper monastery roof during a war against the Fatimids. This group names part of the harbor at Bari due to its role in a conflict against the Normans ended by the Battle of Dyrrhachium ("dir-RACK-ee-um"). Members of this group are responsible for etchings on the side of the Piraeus Lion. This group was first employed to fight Bardas Phokas. As punishment for replacing this group with loyal Scythians, (*) Michael V ("the fifth") was castrated and blinded by Harald Hardrada. Vladimir the Great converted to Orthodoxy and married Anna Porphyrogenita ("POR-fir-uh-JEN-nit-uh") in exchange for providing this group to Basil II ("the second"). This group is named after the Medieval Greek word for Vikings. For 10 points, name this elite force that protected Byzantine emperors.
3.r: Varangian Guard [or Tagma ton Varangon; accept Varangian mercenaries; accept Mare dei Guaranghi; prompt on Vikings or Norsemen until “Vikings” is read]

3.q: The measures that led to this group's downfall were introduced by Georges Couthon and ordered by Marie-Jean Herault. Two of its members, Etienne Claviere and Jean-Marie Roland, became the finance and interior minister; Roland's wife ran a salon that was a gathering-place for this group. This group agitated for the eventual war against (*) Austria, and its leaders included Pierre-Victurnien Vierginaud and Jacques-Pierre Brissot. This group held itself apart from the storming of the Tuilleries, and 29 of its deputies were arrested by Francois Hanriot, most of whom were subsequently guillotined during the Reign of Terror. For 10 points, identify this group of French Revolutionary moderates which hailed from the namesake departement and was opposed by the radical Montagnards.

Members of this group forged friendly relations with Saturiwa and his namesake tribe at their settlement of Fort Caroline, before it was destroyed by Pedro de Aviles ("ah-vee-LACE").
